text:
The road through the pass had been graded and regraded so many times that Oren had lost track of how many miles of it he had walked, but he remembered the trees. The firs that had stood at mile one hundred and forty-one when he was nineteen were gone now, cut for some purpose he never learned, and in their place stood a generation of saplings that had never heard the old road's first trucks.

He had come over the pass on a Tuesday, alone, as he had been alone for the better part of two weeks. His pack was light for autumn: a stove, a thermos, a paperback he had not yet started, and the conviction that a man walking at seventy-one was mostly walking to be somewhere that did not expect anything of him.

The car came down through the pines at mile one hundred and forty-one, which meant he heard it long before he saw it. There was a sound, and a longer sound, and then the silence of things that have finished moving.

He found it forty yards off the shoulder, in the bank below the road, where the guardrail had bent the way wire bends when a man has decided to give up on the fence. The roof had gone down. The windshield was scattered across the road surface. Pine needles had settled on the hood and begun to be dusted with grey, because the clouds were coming down out of the valley the way they do when the season is deciding to become winter.

The woman was in the driver's seat, or had been, in the way a person is in a seat when the seat has stopped being much of anything. She lay on her side against the mangled door, head at an angle that made her neck look like a question. Grey wool coat, boots with good soles, dark hair gone grey at the temples, loose over her face.

Oren stood above her for a while without moving, the way you stand at the edge of a deep pool. Then he went down the bank, put his hand to her throat and found nothing there, and put his ear where her chest should have been making its small argument for going on, and it was not making any argument at all. The cold had a way of making everything honest, and this was honest.

She had been driving south. He could tell from the gradient and the way the car had come down. He wanted that fact to mean something, to be a direction he could follow with her, but it was only a fact.

His phone had one bar of signal, the one bar he had been carrying all week like a small lit window. It took so long to connect that he thought the wilderness had swallowed the call. Then a voice answered, female, unhurried, and asked where he was.

"Mile one hundred and forty-one. Off the shoulder, in the bank. One vehicle. One person inside."

"Are you injured, sir?"

"No. I'm walking."

There was a pause that he took to be her thinking about him, a seventy-one-year-old man walking alone in a pass with a dead woman beside him. She asked him to stay with her. Keep her warm. Someone was being dispatched. The road was not plowed. The pass was not friendly to anyone right now. It would take time.

"Okay," he said. "I'll stay."

She stayed with him, he stayed with her, and the light went amber in the firs.

He did what some long-ago course had taught him. He laid his spare wool shirt across her shoulders, because the shirt was warmer than anything he carried and it seemed wrong to leave her uncovered while he stood around in two layers. Her phone was in the glove compartment, which had survived, of all things, and it was dead or locked or both. He did not press it. Some doors you knock on and some you leave.

Then he sat on the guardrail above her, higher ground, less dignified, and began to talk, because the alternative was the wind in the pines, and the wind in the pines was a sound like water moving through a house where nobody lived anymore.

"Your boots," he said. "Good soles. You were coming down from somewhere up north. The pass was already behind you."

He told her about his father, who had driven a logging truck for thirty years on roads like this one, roads with no names, just markers, and who believed a man could know a road the way he knew a face.

"When I was nineteen, my father took me over this pass in August, in the truck, because he wanted me to see the whole of it. He said a road was a promise somebody had made to everybody, and he had kept his part for thirty years. I fell asleep on the passenger seat, which was the wrong thing to do and the right thing at the same time. I woke up at mile one hundred and forty-one. He didn't say anything. No you were sleeping, no you're behind us. He kept driving, we got down into the valley, he made coffee, and we were friends again, or we never had stopped being."

He looked down at the car in the failing light.

"I've been putting words in his mouth for thirty years. Told this story maybe a hundred times, and every time he says something different. Sometimes he says nothing, which is what he actually did, and sometimes some kind thing, which he would never have said, because he wasn't a kind thing man. I think the story changes because he changes, and he's been changing since 1974. I'm the one doing the changing to him."

The snow began then. Not falling at first but standing up, drifting sideways out of the cloud that had filled the valley and was climbing the far slope, so the world began to be drawn in, edge by edge.

He went down to her, adjusted the shirt, sat in the bank with his back against the tire.

He told her about the summer his brother drowned at the lake, which was not a beautiful lake, and which he did not go near anymore. The men with the nets came back up the bank empty-handed. His mother sat on the porch with a blanket she was not cold enough to need. His brother had been twenty-six and had been, as far as he knew, in no particular hurry to be anywhere.

"That's the thing nobody tells you," he said. "The impermanence isn't in the dying. It's in the after. Everything keeps going at exactly the speed it was going. The nets get rolled up. The porch light gets turned off. The lake fills with the next summer's fishermen. You stand there holding something that just stopped, and the world does not hold it with you."

He told her briefly about his first wife, a woman named Dot, who had left in the spring of 1989 to go be a better person somewhere warmer and had sent one postcard and then nothing.

"I hope she got there," he said. "I hope it was a warm place."

Then the surveyor, an old man with a brass rod who had told him every line he ran was temporary, that the land shifted a fraction of a degree every year, and that this was not a disappointment but the entire job.

"I think about that man a lot," Oren said. "I think that's the whole of it. You measure. You hold what you have while it holds still. And then you measure again, somewhere else."

He had stopped saying her name in his head because he did not know it. He could be keeping company for hours with a person and not have one fact about her except good boots and southbound. He wondered what she had been reading. There was a book somewhere in the wreckage, or in the glove box, or on the passenger seat, which was now part of the floor.

The dark came the way it comes in mountains: not gradually but as a decision. One moment the pines had color, and the next they were shapes, and the road was a rumor, and the pass was a sound rather than a place. The snow fell properly now, thick flakes the wind pushed against the car like a crowd trying to get in. He covered her face with his glove, which was absurd, but the gesture seemed necessary.

Lights came through the pines at half past nine, orange and white, cutting the snowfall into visible falling, a strange beauty, snow beautiful when something shines through it and ordinary when it just falls.

A truck stopped above the bank, then a second vehicle. Men came down with straps and a stretcher and the brisk unhurriedness of people who had done this and would do it again. They were careful with her, and Oren felt himself gently moved aside, a man who had sat too long in the way of the ambulance.

A woman with a headlamp and a clipboard asked if he was sure, in the tone of someone confirming an address.

"I've been talking to her," Oren said. "For two hours. If she had wanted to say something, she would have had the chance."

She looked at him for a moment, nodded, wrote something down.

They loaded her up. The snow was falling on the stretcher, on the trees, and the pass was falling in on itself, mile by mile, marker by marker. The paramedic asked for his name for the report. It went onto the clipboard and would sit there for a while, true only for a while, like the surveyor's lines.

He helped carry the stretcher to the truck, doing it before he had decided to, and stood on the road and watched the lights go south, up into the trees, swallowed.

"Excuse me," he said, to the last paramedic, who was packing the stretcher away. "There was a book. Somewhere in the car. I didn't see it."

The man looked at the darkened shell of the vehicle. "We'll find it. We'll get it to her family."

"Good," Oren said. "I was hoping to know what she was reading."

He stood a while longer in the snow, at mile one hundred and forty-one, which was still mile one hundred and forty-one, one of the few things that had stayed. Then he turned north, the way he had come, into the wind in the young firs, and walked.
